function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

We can use the cmd_controller_execute function to run a command that checks for installed VPNs. On Windows, we could query installed programs via WMIC or PowerShell. For example, we can run:

powershell "Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_Product | Where-Object { $_.Name -match 'VPN' }"

But maybe simpler: use wmic product get name. Or use Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*.

We can run a command that lists installed programs and grep for VPN. But Windows doesn't have grep. Use findstr.

Command: wmic product get Name | findstr /i "vpn"

Alternatively, use PowerShell: Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* | Select-Object DisplayName | findstr /i "vpn"

But findstr is a command-line tool. In PowerShell, we can pipe to findstr. But we can also use Where-Object.

Simpler: powershell "Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\\Software\\Wow6432Node\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\* | Where-Object {$_.DisplayName -match 'vpn'} | Select-Object DisplayName"

powershell "Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\\Software\\Wow6432Node\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\* | Where-Object {$_.DisplayName -match 'vpn'} | Select-Object DisplayName" && powershell "Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\* | Where-Object {$_.DisplayName -match 'vpn'} | Select-Object DisplayName"

Let's craft a command:
